description: Hi, I'm Ho Qi Yuan, a final-year Data Science student at Multimedia University, Malaysia, competing solo in the Johor Bahru virtual event. I'm taking on "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" with an idea borrowed from ecology: treat each satellite pass like a wildlife survey and estimate the fires every sensor missed, so 20+ years of fire records can be compared fairly. Skills: Python, statistics, FastAPI, Next.js and 3D web design.
summary: FireCensus turns 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one consistent fire record for Southeast Asia (2002–2026), so the sensor that saw a fire no longer matters. MODIS misses most of the small fires VIIRS sees, so simply joining the records creates a fake 4.4× jump in 2012. Instead of converting one sensor into the other with a ratio, we borrow capture–recapture statistics from ecology: each satellite pass is treated like a wildlife survey, and how often satellites see the same fire tells us how many fires all of them missed. The harmonized count barely moves when a satellite is removed (0–6% vs 15–25% for raw counts) and works with VIIRS alone, so the record can continue after MODIS ends in 2027. Our web app tells this as one story on a 3D globe: pick a region or draw your own area to get a burning calendar, anomalies versus history, the fire season, every individual fire, a 2002–2026 timelapse and CSV downloads.
details:
1. Summary

FireCensus turns 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one consistent fire record for Southeast Asia (July 2002 – November 2026), where the satellite of origin no longer matters. Instead of converting one sensor into the other with a ratio, we borrow capture–recapture statistics from ecology to estimate how many fires burned, including the ones no satellite detected.

2. How We Addressed the Challenge

What it does: MODIS (1 km pixels) misses most of the small fires that VIIRS (375 m) sees, so a naive record jumps ×4.4 in 2012 when VIIRS arrives. FireCensus produces one VIIRS-equivalent fire count for every 0.1° cell and month, whichever satellites were flying, and serves it in an interactive website.

How it works: We treat each satellite pass like a wildlife survey. Fires seen by Aqua MODIS, S-NPP VIIRS and NOAA-20 VIIRS are matched within 1.5 km in the same afternoon window (12:30–15:30 local solar time), giving each fire a "capture history", e.g. (1,0,1) = seen by Aqua and NOAA-20, missed by S-NPP. A Huggins capture–recapture model learns each satellite's detection curve from fire heat (FRP) and pixel size. Horvitz–Thompson weighting (N = Σ 1/p*) then adds back the fires every satellite missed. For 2002–2011, when only MODIS flew, a back-cast factor learned from the 2012–2021 overlap restores what MODIS cannot see. 2026 is processed from near-real-time data with the same model.

Validation: dropping one satellite changes raw counts by 15–25% but FireCensus by only 0–6%; the 2012 jump falls from ×4.4 to −4%; NOAA-21, never used in fitting, behaves like the other VIIRS units; an Australian control region gets only a small correction, so the method does not simply inflate everything. To be honest, the gain on regional totals over a simple ratio is modest (12.5% vs 14.0% median error); our main advantages are stability across satellites, counting unseen fires, and continuity after MODIS.

The website (https://firecensus-rho.vercel.app) tells this as one scroll story on a 3D globe. Visitors pick a region, a featured case, or draw their own area, and the globe dives into a NASA Blue Marble map with:

- a "Whose eyes?" lens to compare what Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20 and FireCensus each see, on one colour scale;

- every individual fire when zoomed in, with which satellites saw it and how many unseen fires it stands for;

- a burning calendar and 3D skyline of every month since 2002, this month vs the historical median, the fire season and the worst years;

- "Play the story": seven steps on the map explaining mark–recapture, detection curves, unseen fires, the back-cast and the 2012 test;

- CSV downloads for any area and date range.

Benefits

- One fire record that does not jump when satellites change.

- Counts the fires every satellite missed, cell by cell, which matters most for small peat and farm fires in Southeast Asia.

- Keeps working after MODIS ends in 2027: it runs on VIIRS alone and handled the real S-NPP retirement on 2 November 2026 automatically.

- Explainable: each satellite has a detection curve with physical meaning, and every number can be traced back to individual detections.

- Usable without coding by early-warning teams, researchers and land managers.

How It Is Creative

Other approaches convert one sensor into the other. As far as we could find, FireCensus is the first to apply capture–recapture, a method ecologists use to count fish and birds, to MODIS/VIIRS fire records. It turns the disagreement between satellites into information: how often two satellites see the same fire tells us how many fires all of them missed. More satellites make the estimate better, not more confusing.

Factors We Considered

Fires appear and disappear within minutes, so we define the estimate as fires burning during the afternoon window and learned detection from the closest-in-time satellite pairs. We treated a satellite that did not pass over as "missing", not as a miss; capped weights so one faint detection cannot dominate; masked static heat sources in near-real-time data; used one calibration period for all years so trends are comparable; and stated our limits openly: pre-2012 single cells are noisy, the estimate is conservative, and night and morning passes are not yet modelled.

What We Hope to Achieve

We want the 25-year MODIS fire record to survive the end of MODIS, so that early-warning teams, haze researchers and land managers in Southeast Asia can compare this year's fires with the past fairly. Next steps: add night passes and Terra's morning pass, extend the method to other regions, link fire counts to burned area and haze emissions, and run it daily on FIRMS near-real-time data.

Tools and Technologies

- Languages: Python (data pipeline and models), TypeScript (website), SQL (DuckDB).

- Data and statistics: pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (DBSCAN clustering), statsmodels, DuckDB, Apache Parquet.

- Backend: FastAPI. Website: Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, Spline (3D globe), react-three-fiber; hosted on Vercel.

- 3D assets: NASA Blue Marble textures and NASA 3D Resources satellite models, prepared in Blender.

- Hardware: a standard laptop.

- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) for research, coding, analysis and writing, disclosed in the README.

3. How We Used Space Agency Data

All fire data come from NASA FIRMS: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m active fires (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), standard and near-real-time, about 61 million detections for Southeast Asia from 2002 to 2026. The map uses NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery; the 3D globe uses NASA Blue Marble Next Generation textures; the satellites are NASA 3D Resources models. We acknowledge the use of data and imagery from LANCE FIRMS, operated by NASA's Earth Science Data and Information System (ESDIS), with funding provided by NASA Headquarters.
